readerTitle: The camera is 90% accurate. Most parts it rejects are fine.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (부품 공장 검사 카메라, 앱 가입 사기 탐지) + 실제 연구 (Tversky & Kahneman 택시 문제) · 공장·앱 수치는 설명용
insight: 경보나 증거를 보기 전에, 그 일이 원래 얼마나 자주 일어나는지부터 묻는다. 드문 일일수록 경보의 대부분은 오경보다.
misconception: 검사가 90% 정확하면, 검사에 걸린 것도 90% 확률로 진짜 문제다.

sources.text: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1982). Evidential impact of base rates. In Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky (Eds.), Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Cambridge University Press.
공장 검사 카메라와 앱 가입 사기 탐지 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 공장 계산: 부품 10,000개, 불량률 1% = 불량 100개, 정상 9,900개. 카메라가 불량의 90%를 잡음 = 90개. 정상품의 5%를 잘못 걸러냄 = 495개. 걸린 부품 합계 585개, 그중 진짜 불량 90 ÷ 585 = 15.4%(약 15%). 정상품 비율 495 ÷ 585 = 84.6%.
택시 문제: 택시의 85% 초록, 15% 파랑, 목격자 정확도 80%. 파랑이고 파랑이라 말함 0.15 × 0.8 = 0.12, 초록인데 파랑이라 말함 0.85 × 0.2 = 0.17. 0.12 ÷ 0.29 = 41.4%(약 41%). 다수 응답이 80%였다는 점은 원문에서 문구를 다시 확인하세요.
앱 계산: 월 가입 20,000건, 사기 1/200 = 100건, 정상 19,900건. 도구가 사기 95건을 잡고 정상의 2%를 잘못 표시 = 398건. 표시된 계정 493건 중 사기 95 ÷ 493 = 19.3%(약 1/5). 표시군의 사기 비율은 전체(0.5%)의 약 39배(19.3 ÷ 0.5).

cards.title: The camera is 90% accurate. Most parts it rejects are fine.
body: A parts factory installs a new inspection camera. It catches 90% of defective parts.
Within a week, the reject bin is overflowing, and the line workers swear most of those parts look perfect. They are right. The camera works as promised. The problem is a number nobody looked at.

image.label: Overflowing reject bin next to a conveyor camera
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 컨베이어 벨트 위 금속 부품들, 위에 검사 카메라. 옆의 빨간 불량품 통이 넘칠 만큼 가득 차 있고, 작업자가 부품 하나를 들어 고개를 갸웃함. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: The camera flags a part. Is it defective?
body: About 1 in 100 parts from this line is truly defective. The camera catches 90% of those. It also wrongly flags 5% of good parts.
A part lands in the reject bin. How likely is it to be truly defective?

options.feedback: That's how often the camera catches a bad part, not how often a flagged part is bad. Those are different questions.
Good instinct that false alarms matter. But good parts outnumber bad ones 99 to 1, so false alarms matter even more than that.
Right. Because defects are rare, false alarms on good parts swamp the real catches. The next card shows the count.

cards.title: Follow 10,000 parts.
cards.callout: The camera is good. Defects are just rare, so most of its alarms come from the huge pile of good parts.
cards.softwareNote: The same math hits spam filters, error alerts and fraud checks. When the thing you hunt is rare, even a small false-alarm rate can bury the real cases.

cards.title: Base rates
body: A **base rate** is how often something happens in the whole group, before you look at the case in front of you. Here, it's 1 defect in 100 parts.
People tend to skip it. A specific signal, like a camera alarm, feels more real than a dull background number. This is called **base rate neglect**.
But the background number decides how much the signal means. Start there.

image.label: Small red dots among a large crowd of gray dots
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 회색 점 99개와 빨간 점 1개로 이루어진 격자. 그 위에 돋보기 하나가 몇 개의 점을 비추고 있음. 제목 "Start with how common it is".

cards.title: The taxi problem
body: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman gave people a puzzle. In a city, 85% of taxis are green and 15% are blue. A witness says a hit-and-run cab was blue. Tests show the witness is right 80% of the time.
Many people answered that the cab was 80% likely to be blue. The math says about **41%**. Green cabs are so common that a witness's mistakes about them outweigh the correct sightings of blue ones.

image.label: Many green taxis and a few blue ones on a street
image.brief: 밤거리 일러스트. 초록 택시가 많고 파란 택시는 몇 대뿐. 한쪽에 목격자가 손가락으로 가리키는 모습. 실제 택시 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Ask the boring question first.
body: Before you judge a single case, ask how often cases like it turn out a certain way.
list: A new hire with a great interview: how often do great interviews predict great work here?
A late-paying customer: how often do customers like this one never pay?
A bold expansion plan: how often do plans like this hit their targets?
cards.callout: The story in front of you is vivid. The base rate is usually more reliable.

cards.title: The right group matters.
body: A base rate is only useful if it comes from a group like yours. Defect rates from a different line, or last year's machine, can mislead you.
It's also a starting point, not the final answer. Strong, specific evidence should move your view. How much it should move is the topic of a later lesson on updating beliefs.
And base rates change. Recheck them when your process, market or customers change.

cards.title: Now it's a fraud filter on an app.
body: Your app gets 20,000 signups a month. About 1 in 200 is fraud. A new tool catches 95% of fraud but also flags 2% of genuine users.
That's about 490 flagged accounts a month, and only about 1 in 5 is fraud. What do you do with them?

options.feedback: You stop almost all fraud, but you also lock out about 400 real customers a month. Many won't come back.

options.text: Send flagged accounts to a quick extra check, like card verification
options.feedback: The flag concentrates fraud, from 0.5% to about 20%, so it's worth acting on. A light check stops fraud without punishing the real users.

options.text: Ignore the tool, since most of its flags are wrong
options.feedback: True that most flags are false. But flagged accounts are about 39 times more likely to be fraud than average. That's useful.

cards.title: Before trusting a signal, ask how common the thing is.
body: When something is rare, most alarms about it are false, even from a good test. Use the alarm to decide where to look, not as the verdict.
**Try it today:** pick one alert or check your business relies on. Count how many of its last 20 flags turned out to be real.
